advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Re-anchor test_canonical_explicit_assignee_guidance_is_conditional_on_jira on a canonical identifier (e.g. `--assignee`) rather than prose fragments that break on a behavior-preserving reword.
evidence: Rule-5 litmus: 'a prose/heading grep that merely guards the author's wording IS a change-detector'; all three tokens are prose fragments, none is a CLI command, config key, or relation identifier read by a non-human consumer.
tests/unit/test_client_template_sync.py:121: assert "claimed ticket remains unassigned" in text

These substrings are prose sentence-fragments, not canonical identifiers read by a non-human consumer; a reword preserving the guidance (e.g. 'the ticket stays unassigned') fails the test with no contract change (Rule-4 refactoring-violation litmus).
advisory.finding: test_canonical_explicit_assignee_guidance_is_conditional_on_jira asserts only prose sentence-fragments ('Jira-reconciled store', 'explicit override', 'email or accountId') with no canonical identifier (command name, config key, or relation) anchoring the check. These are author-wording greps: a behavior-preserving reword that keeps the same guidance (e.g. 'when the store reconciles with Jira, supply a resolvable account') would break the test without any change to the actual guidance contract. Per the Rule-5 litmus, an LLM consumer is not a non-human consumer, so this is a change-detector, not a structural-boundary assertion.
